summary: Nainen sen tietää by Kaarle Halme is a three-act play written in the early 20th century. It follows young writer Kauko Helotie, his fiancée Sirkku, and her returning father, engineer Mauri Suvialho, as love collides with family pride, inheritance, and a cloud of doubt over paternity. The story weighs personal honor against money and control, with the shadow of colonial hardship darkening family ties. The opening of the play introduces Sirkku in Kauko’s modest flat on midsummer eve: she reveals their fresh engagement and her long-absent father’s sudden return from Africa. Kauko, irritated by his wealthy uncle Malkala’s theatrics about dying, learns of a will Sirkku typed that names him heir “if” he is truly the brother’s son—an insinuation that outrages him as a slur on his mother. Mauri arrives, hints at hard years in Congo and old entanglements with the Malkalas, then reacts with shock to the engagement and later demands the couple break it off, refusing to give reasons and vowing to stop the match by money or force. Kauko counters by posting the banns immediately; Mauri tries to lure Sirkku abroad, and, failing that, secretly hires a closed car and arranges passage on a night boat, implying an attempt to spirit her away. As Malkala dies and the will stands, Kauko and Sirkku calmly plan to confirm the banns and keep her safe for the night, while Mauri stealthily searches Sirkku’s drawer for a sealed letter from her late mother before confronting Kauko again—the scene ending in mounting tension.
